Newton's First Law — The Law of Inertia
An object remains at rest, or continues to move in a straight line at constant speed, unless acted upon by a resultant force.
This law makes two important statements:
If the resultant force on an object is zero
, the object either stays still or continues moving at the same speed in the same direction. There is no change in velocity — the object is in
If the resultant force is not zero
, the velocity of the object will change — it will accelerate, decelerate, or change direction.
is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of motion. The more massive an object is, the greater its inertia.
Everyday examples of Newton's first law:
When a car stops suddenly, your body tends to continue moving forward (due to inertia). A seatbelt provides the resultant force needed to decelerate your body along with the car.
A coin on a piece of card:
Place a coin on a card on top of a glass. Flick the card quickly sideways. The card flies off, but the coin drops straight into the glass — its inertia means it resists the sideways motion.
A spacecraft far from any gravitational field will continue in a straight line at constant speed without needing its engines. There is no resultant force, so no change in velocity.
Pulling a tablecloth quickly from under dishes works because the dishes have inertia — they resist the sudden change in motion.
The resultant force acting on an object is equal to the product of the object's mass and its acceleration. The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.

So one newton is the force required to give a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².

Newton's Third Law — Action and Reaction
When object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal and opposite force on object A.
(or Newton's third law pairs). They have the following characteristics:
The two forces in a Newton's third law pair act on
Your foot pushes backward on the ground (action). The ground pushes forward on your foot (reaction). This forward push is what moves you forward.
A swimmer pushes water backward with their hands (action). The water pushes the swimmer forward (reaction).

The rocket pushes exhaust gases downward (action). The exhaust gases push the rocket upward (reaction). This works even in the vacuum of space because the rocket pushes against its own exhaust, not against the air.
The book pushes down on the table with its weight (action). The table pushes up on the book with a normal contact force (reaction).
The Earth pulls the Moon toward it with gravitational force (action). The Moon pulls the Earth toward it with an equal gravitational force (reaction).
A helpful method is to use the phrase: "Object A pushes/pulls object B, so object B pushes/pulls object A."
For example: "The book pushes the table downward, so the table pushes the book upward."

(a) Calculate the deceleration of the car. (b) Explain what happens to the passengers if they are not wearing seatbelts.
(a) The braking force acts opposite to the direction of motion.

(b) By Newton's first law, the passengers' bodies tend to continue moving forward at 20 m/s (due to inertia). Without seatbelts, there is no force to decelerate the passengers, so they would continue moving forward and could hit the dashboard or windscreen. Seatbelts provide the necessary restraining force to decelerate the passengers along with the car.
"A force is needed to keep an object moving at constant speed."
This is perhaps the most common misconception in physics. Newton's first law tells us that an object moving at constant speed in a straight line has

. On Earth, we often need to apply a force to maintain motion only because we need to overcome friction and air resistance — the applied force balances the resistive forces, making the resultant force zero. In the absence of friction (e.g., in space), no force is needed to maintain motion.
"Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects."
In a vacuum, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass, because

for all objects. In air, objects with different shapes and sizes experience different amounts of air resistance, which can make them fall at different rates — but this is due to air resistance, not mass. A heavy ball and a light ball of the same size and shape will fall at almost the same rate in air.
Newton's third law pairs act on
, so they cannot cancel each other out. Forces can only cancel when they act on the

. For example, a book on a table: the weight (Earth pulls book) and normal force (table pushes book) act on the same object and can balance. But the weight of the book and the Earth being pulled by the book are a third law pair acting on different objects.
"If an object is at rest, no forces act on it."

An object at rest may have many forces acting on it — but those forces are balanced (the resultant force is zero). A book on a table has weight acting downward and the normal force acting upward. The forces are there, but they cancel to give a zero resultant.
"The resultant force is always in the direction of motion."
The resultant force is in the direction of

, not necessarily in the direction of motion. A car braking has a resultant force opposite to its direction of motion. A ball thrown upward has a resultant downward force (gravity) even while it is still moving upward.
"Mass and weight are the same thing."

Mass is measured in kilograms and does not change with location. Weight is a force measured in newtons and depends on the gravitational field strength. An object with a mass of 10 kg weighs about 100 N on Earth but only about 16 N on the Moon.
"Newton's third law means forces are always balanced."

Newton's third law tells us that forces come in pairs, but this does not mean that the forces on any particular object are balanced. A rocket accelerates upward because the upward thrust on the rocket is greater than its weight — the forces on the rocket are unbalanced, even though Newton's third law still holds for every interaction.

An object remains at rest, or continues to move in a straight line at constant speed, unless acted upon by a resultant force.

When the bus suddenly accelerates forward, the passenger's body tends to remain at rest due to inertia (Newton's first law). Since no forward force is initially applied to the upper body, it stays behind while the feet (in contact with the bus floor via friction) move forward with the bus. The passenger therefore appears to lurch backward relative to the bus.
A more powerful engine can produce a greater driving force. By Newton's second law (
), if the mass is the same, a greater resultant force produces a greater acceleration. Therefore the car with the more powerful engine accelerates faster.

When the skydiver first jumps, their weight is much greater than air resistance, so there is a large resultant downward force. By Newton's second law, the skydiver accelerates. As speed increases, air resistance increases. The resultant force decreases, so acceleration decreases. Eventually, air resistance equals the weight, so the resultant force is zero. By Newton's first law, the skydiver now moves at constant velocity — this is terminal velocity.

Newton's third law: when object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal and opposite force on object A. Example: when you push a wall (your hand exerts a force on the wall), the wall pushes back on your hand with an equal force in the opposite direction. The action force acts on the wall; the reaction force acts on your hand.

On the rough surface, friction provides a resultant force opposing the ball's motion. By Newton's first law, this unbalanced force causes the ball to decelerate and eventually stop. On the very smooth surface, friction is much smaller, so the resultant force opposing motion is smaller. The ball decelerates much more slowly and travels further before stopping. If friction were zero, the ball would continue at constant speed indefinitely.

By Newton's third law, if the car exerts a forward force on the trailer, the trailer exerts an equal backward force on the car. The car can still accelerate forward because the driving force from the road on the car's wheels (due to the engine) is greater than the backward pull from the trailer. The resultant force on the car is therefore forward, so by Newton's second law, the car accelerates forward.

Astronauts on the ISS are in freefall — they and the space station are both falling toward Earth at the same rate (they are in orbit, which is continuous freefall). Because the astronaut and the station accelerate identically, there is no contact force between the astronaut and the floor. The astronaut's weight still exists (gravity is only slightly weaker at ISS altitude), but there is no normal reaction force — so the astronaut feels weightless.
